s1.quote: stretches from the shallows down to over 80m deep … All diving here requires surface support because of strong currents and the potential to be swept off the reef. … Only liveaboard boats can dive the Brothers

s2.quote: The wreck starts at 8 meters/26 ft. with the stem of the boat, but the ship's main body starts around 20 meters/65 ft. The Stern is around 80 meters/260 ft. … The currents on both wrecks can be severe. … 30-meter-plus (100-feet) visibility

hazards.text: Strong current, risk of being swept off the reef

summary.text: A long steamship wreck on the Big Brother reef, reached only by liveaboard. The bow sits near 8 m while the hull falls past 80 m, so most divers see the upper sections in a current that can be fierce.

s1.quote: The currents on both wrecks can be severe. … A serious, current-exposed dive best suited to experienced wreck divers.

s2.quote: stretching from 25 meters to 60 metres from bow to stern

s3.quote: Only liveaboard boats can dive the Brothers

summary.text: A small supply ship wrecked on the Brothers reef and now lying on a steep slope. It is a demanding, current-swept dive for experienced wreck divers, reachable only from liveaboards.

s1.quote: The stern section lies at a 45-degree angle, resting on its port side at about 24 meters deep. … The 'A-frame' mast reaches toward the surface, encrusted in soft corals and surrounded by swirling clouds of glassfish and hunting trevally.

s2.quote: The deepest part of the stern lies in just 24m … penetrate deep into the engine-room, crew's quarters and bridge

s3.quote: the Giannis D's mast reaches to about 13 ft (4 m) with its stern near 79 ft (24 m) … the current funneling through the Gulf of Suez here can be strong

highlights.text: Glassfish clouds and trevally around the mast
Engine room, crew quarters and bridge to explore

hazards.text: Current can be strong and shift quickly

summary.text: A large cargo ship lying on its side on Abu Nuhas reef, with the mast near the surface and the stern around 24 m. Experienced wreck divers can swim into the engine room and bridge, though the tilt is disorienting.

s1.quote: now lies on its port side in 26m, rising to 12m at the bow … penetration is simple because of all the entry/exit points through the iron framework

s2.quote: the Carnatic sits around 59-89 ft (18-27 m) … the current funneling through the Gulf of Suez here can be strong

s3.quote: purple and orange sea fans cover every inch of the remaining ribs

penetration.value: Easy entry and exit through the open iron framework

highlights.text: Sea fans covering the skeletal ribs

hazards.text: Current can be strong and shift quickly

summary.text: A 19th-century iron steamship wreck on Abu Nuhas, resting on its port side with the bow far shallower than the stern. The open framework is easy to swim through and heavily covered in sea fans and coral.

s1.quote: The bow is remarkably shallow, sitting in just 3 to 5 meters of water … thousands of tiles still neatly stacked in their crates

s2.quote: sitting in 26m-28m … Full penetration is possible in certain areas for experienced wreck-divers

s3.quote: the Chrisoula K spans roughly 13-92 ft (4-28 m) … the current funneling through the Gulf of Suez here can be strong

penetration.value: Full penetration possible in certain areas for experienced wreck divers

highlights.text: Cargo of floor tiles still stacked in crates

hazards.text: Current can be strong and shift quickly

summary.text: An upright cargo freighter on Abu Nuhas whose bow almost reaches the surface and whose stern rests near 28 m. Its hold still contains stacked tiles and experienced wreck divers can enter parts of the interior.

s1.quote: large groupers, schooling snappers, and the occasional resident turtle

s2.quote: slid off the reef into 30-32m of water … relatively easy to get into the engineering department, and from there into the holds

s3.quote: the Kimon M is the deepest, with sections down to around 100 ft (30 m) or more … the current funneling through the Gulf of Suez here can be strong

penetration.value: Engineering department and holds are fairly easy to enter

hazards.text: Current can be strong and shift quickly

summary.text: The deepest of the four Abu Nuhas wrecks, a freighter that slid off the reef to rest around 30 m. Divers can reach the engine spaces and holds, and groupers and snappers gather on the hull.

s1.quote: wall reaching from the surface to 18m … a column of Gorgonian Fans that reaches from 14 to 28m

s2.quote: currents can be strong … fantastic giant sea fan collections

highlights.text: Column of gorgonian fans from 14 to 28 m

summary.text: A fringing reef beneath the Ras Umm Sid lighthouse near Sharm el Sheikh, known for a band of large gorgonian sea fans along the wall and a coral garden on the plateau. Currents can pick up, so a drift suits it.

s1.quote: within a 12m depth range … perfect dive site for all diving levels … only possible on a very calm day due to it's location and shallow depth

s2.quote: wrecked in the Straits of Tiran in the Red Sea on 21 August 1984

hazards.text: Dive only possible on very calm days

summary.text: A shallow cargo ship wreck lying in the Straits of Tiran since 1984, with its winch, engine and propeller all within about 12 m. Suitable for all levels but accessible only in very calm weather.

s1.quote: 5-35M … Beginner … Always sheltered and very busy on a windy day … A terrace-profiled plateau next to a shallow wall at the very south tip of Abu Ramada Island

The coral cascades down from the reef top towards the seabed 14 meters below … Regardless of the sometimes strong currents, this location is suitable for every diving level. … Boats moor on the southern reef side

mooring.value: Boats moor on the southern reef side

s1.quote: max. 16 m … the massive cave opening at 12 metres

s2.quote: between 6 and 9 metres … an expansive and spectacular system of caves … strong currents

highlights.text: Shallow cave system with light shafts

summary.text: A shallow reef in the Fury Shoals with a spacious, partly open-roofed cave network, popular for sunbeams and photography. Maximum depth is about 16 m, though currents can be strong on the approach.
